background.definition: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an acquired autoimmune disease affecting the neuromuscular junction. It is characterized by the formation of antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) and fatigable weakness. Myasthenic syndromes, distinctly different disease entities, are genetic or acquired disorders of neuromuscular transmission associated with abnormal weakness and fatigability on exertion. However, myasthenic syndromes have etiologies that are different from MG. Myasthenic syndromes include the Lambert-Eaton syndrome, congenital myasthenic syndromes, and toxic or drug-induced disorders of neuromuscular transmission.

list.listitem: As many as 2 per 100,000 population are newly diagnosed with MG each year. The incidence varies markedly from region to region.
In the United States, approximately 20 per 100,000 population suffer from MG.
MG is characterized by the production of AChR antibodies that block the postsynaptic receptors at the neuromuscular junctions.
Although MG has been associated with hyperplasia of the thymus and thymoma, the immunologic mechanism of antibody production in MG is still not well understood.
The association of different types of MG with specific human leukocyte antigen implies that the susceptibility to develop MG is genetically controlled.
summarizes conditions and drugs that may exacerbate MG.
MG is associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially of the thyroid.
Complement fixing antibodies against the α-1 muscle nicotinic AChR or associated molecules results in altered function of the neuromuscular junction through loss of AChR.
This contributes to the symptoms of fatigability and weakness in ocular, bulbar, respiratory, and skeletal muscle groups.

list.listitem: The Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America classification of MG is summarized in . It is designed to identify subgroups of patients with MG who share distinct clinical features or severity of disease.

Patients typically present with fatigability and weakness of muscles, which increases during repeated use and improves with rest or sleep. Other symptoms include diplopia and ptosis, facial weakness that results in a snarl-like expression when smiling, nasal timbre during speech, and difficulty in swallowing.
Patients with generalized myasthenia will often have asymmetric and proximal weakness in the limb muscles.

On physical examination, deep tendon reflexes and sensation are preserved, and there is a lack of other neurologic signs. Weakness on physical examination is the hallmark of MG. This can be elicited, for example, by having the patient hold both arms straight forward and abducted for 5 minutes.

Perform the ice test by placing a bag of crushed ice over the ptotic eyelid for 2 minutes. Complete or almost complete resolution of ptosis or at least a 2-mm increase in palpebral fissure width constitutes a positive response.

Perform the sleep test by leaving the patient in a quiet dark room with the eyes closed for 30 minutes. Complete or almost complete resolution of ptosis or at least a 2-mm increase in palpebral fissure width constitutes a positive response.
Peek sign: after gentle eyelid closure, the eyelid margins quickly separate and the sclera start to show.
To perform the edrophonium (Tensilon) test, give 2 to 8 mg of edrophonium IV. A positive result is when objective improvement occurs.
Positive ice test, peek sign, sleep test, or edrophonium (Tensilon) test are virtually diagnostic of MG.
Anti-AChR antibodies are very specific but not sensitive. The presence of antibodies results in a definitive diagnosis, but their absence does not exclude MG.
Antibodies against the muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase (anti-MuSK) are present in 70% of patients who lack AChR antibodies.
The repetitive nerve stimulation test, is more accurate in generalized MG than in ocular MG.

A positive repetitive nerve stimulation test is useful for diagnosis of ocular myasthenia and generalized myasthenia. It is defined as more than a 10% decrease in amplitude of the muscle action potential when stimulated at 3 to 5 Hz.
Patients may present with different patterns of muscle involvement (ocular, oropharyngeal, or generalized MG).

The diagnosis of MG can be made by demonstrating: weakness of voluntary muscles (including those innervated by cranial nerves); fluctuating weakness or fatigability; and an objective improvement with anticholinesterase drugs (eg, edrophonium test).

The diagnosis is supported by either (1) anti-AChR antibody levels greater than 1 nM; or (2) decremental electromyographic response (at least 10% decrease in the amplitude of the muscle action potential when stimulated at 3-5 Hz); or (3) positive single-fiber electromyography (mean jitter >20 microseconds).

Patients in whom long-term immunosuppression is necessary, azathioprine is recommended together with steroids to allow tapering the steroids to the lowest possible dose while maintaining azathioprine. B
Thymectomy improves outcomes regardless of severity of MG or the presence of thymoma.B
Patients with ocular or generalized MG should initially be treated with anticholinesterase drugs.Those patients with poor responses should be started on immunosuppressive drugs.

Anticholinesterase drugs (eg, pyridostigmine 300-1200 mg/d in divided doses) should be the first drugs used.Patients usually experience partial improvement; complete improvement occurs in few patients. These drugs do not stop the natural progression of disease state. Muscarinic side effects (eg, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, etc.) may limit the tolerated dose.

Although the evidence base for their use is weak, oral corticosteroids are considered first-line drugs for short-term benefit when immunosuppressive drugs are necessary. Since early deterioration may be seen in one-third of patients on corticosteroids, start at a low dose (eg, prednisolone 15-25 mg/d). Then increase the dose slowly until marked clinical improvement occurs. Maintain this dose for 1 to 3 months and then, if possible, reduce to an alternate-day regimen.

Patients in whom long-term immunosuppression is necessary, azathioprine and cyclosporine allow tapering the steroids to lower doses to decrease steroid-induced complications. It may take up to 6 months to see beneficial effects.

Mycophenolate mofetil has been shown in pilot studies to improve functional status or has been used as a steroid-sparing agent. It may be better tolerated than other immunomodulators due to its relative lack of side effects. It may become the drug of choice for long-term therapy. Beneficial effects may take many months and up to a year to be seen.

A prospective chort study enrolled 167 patients with MG who had not previously been treated with an immunosuppressant, of whom 47 received mycophenolate, 31 received azathioprine, and 85 received neither with a mean follow-up of 20 to 25 months. There was no difference in clinical scores or response between the two active treatment groups. They found that lower doses of azathioprine appeared to be similarly effective to higher doses and may cause less hepatotoxicity.
Mycophosphenate and methotrexate have less hepatotoxicity than azathioprine in a survey of 235 patients taking one of the three drugs.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be used to treat moderate-to-severe MG or MG crisis or to prevent deterioration prior to thymectomy. A Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of IVIG.

IVIG and plasma exchange are equally effective for the treatment of MG exacerbations. Rapid improvement occurs in 70% of patients within 4 to 5 days of treatment. The beneficial effect may last for weeks to months.
There is no apparent benefit for methotrexate use. Use of methotrexate does not decrease steroid use.
Retrospecitve data show there may be a role for rituximab in treatment. RCTs are needed before wide implementation.

This monoclonal antibody inebilizumab was modestly effective for generalized myasthenia gravis in an RCT with 236 patients, but only if you taper steroids down to 5 mg per day in the comparison group.
Tacrolimus may be a treatment option but more data are needed.
Once thymoma is diagnosed, thymectomy is indicated regardless of the severity of MG.

For patients with nonthymomatous autoimmune MG, thymectomy is recommended as an option to increase the probability of remission or improvement. This is based largely on a randomized trial of 126 patients with nonthymomatous MGfollowed for 3 years who were randomized to thymectomy alone or thymectomy plus prednisone. Symptoms, exacerbations, and the need for immunosuppression were all significantly improved.
Plasma exchange is recommended as a short-term treatment in MG, especially in severe cases to induce remission and in preparation for surgery.
There is no consensus on the duration of use for anticholinesterase drugs or immunosuppressive agents.
Respiratory failure is a medical emergency that requires intensive care with intubation and mechanical ventilation.
Noninvasive ventilation is an option for less severe respiratory insufficienty.
Respiratory failure can be caused by exacerbation of MG (myasthenic crises) or overdose of cholinesterase inhibitors (cholinergic crises).
Patients negative for anti-AChR and positive for anti-MuSK tend to have oculobulbar weakness and poor response to conventional immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone and azathioprine. B
In a long-term study, the death rate was 33%, remission was seen in 11%, and improvement was seen in 20%. B
Approximately 50% of patients present with pure ocular MG, of whom 50% to 60% will progress to develop generalized MG, mostly in the first 1 to 2 years. B
The natural history of MG is characterized by exacerbations and partial or complete remissions.
Approximately 50% of patients present with pure ocular MG, of whom 50% to 60% will progress to develop generalized MG, mostly in the first 1 to 2 years. B
Patients negative for anti-AChR and positive for anti-MuSK tend to have oculobulbar weakness and poor response to conventional immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone and azathioprine.
In a study following patients whose disease began between 1940 and 1960, the crude death rate was 33%, and remission occurred in 11% and improvement in 20%.
Monitor for other autoimmune disorders including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus erythematosus, Graves' disease, family history of autoimmune disorder, and skin disorders.
Warn patients about conditions or drugs that may exacerbate MG ().
Remind patients to observe for any increase of weakness whenever a new medication is started.
Suggested Web site: Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (http://www.myasthenia.org), Chinese Children's Brain Centre, the University of Hong Kong (http://www.thebraincentre.org/en/).
Between 10% and 20% of infants born to women with MG develop transient neonatal MG and show signs of fetal distress during delivery.
Pregnant women with MG should be examined by a neurologist during pregnancy, to minimize risks and assist in selecting the best mode of delivery.
The risk for neonatal MG will be halved if the mother undergoes thymectomy.
Neonatal MG, from the transplacental transfer of circulating AChR antibodies, persists for several weeks.
Myasthenic disorders in infancy and childhood fall into 2 major categories: autoimmune MG and congenital myasthenic syndromes.
Ocular MG is more common in Asian children and is less likely to progress to the more generalized form. Asian children are also less likely to have AChR antibodies.
In neonates severely affected with MG, IVIG may be a useful adjunct to standard therapy.

feature.caption: Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America Classification of Myasthenia Gravis.
feature.feature_body:
Class Symptoms
I Any ocular muscle weakness
May have weakness of eye closure
All other muscle strength is normal
II Mild weakness affecting other than ocular muscles
May also have ocular muscle weakness of any severity
IIa Predominantly affecting limb or axial muscles, or both
May also have lesser involvement of oropharyngeal muscles
IIb Predominantly affecting oropharyngeal or respiratory muscles, or both
May also have lesser or equal involvement of limb or axial muscles, or both
III Moderate weakness affecting other than ocular muscles
May also have ocular muscle weakness of any severity
IIIa Predominantly affecting limb or axial muscles, or both
May also have lesser involvement of oropharyngeal muscles
IIIb Predominantly affecting oropharyngeal or respiratory muscles, or both
May also have lesser or equal involvement of limb or axial muscles, or both
IV Severe weakness affecting other than ocular muscles
May also have ocular muscle weakness of any severity
IVa Predominantly affecting limb and/or axial muscles
May also have lesser involvement of oropharyngeal muscles
IVb Predominantly affecting oropharyngeal or respiratory muscles, or both
May also have lesser or equal involvement of limb or axial muscles, or both
V Defined by intubation, with or without mechanical ventilation, except when employed during routine postoperative management. The use of a feeding tube without intubation places the patient in class IVb
From Jaretzki A, III, Barohn RJ, Ernstoff RM, et al. Myasthenia gravis: recommendations for clinical research standards. Task Force of the Medical Scientific Advisory Board of the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America. Neurology 2000;55:16–23.
